chapters.body: The bucket waited in the outhouse behind the attap house. Jack Sim was born in 1957 into a poor family in Singapore, the second of three children, and grew up in an impoverished village in Upper Serangoon with no plumbing. Water came from a shared standpipe, and rationing was part of life, with cholera and typhoid moving through the kampong and intestinal worms among children. His father worked as a grocery shop assistant, and the pay could hardly feed three children, their mother and a grandmother. They often wore donated clothes they could not afford to buy. The toilet stood outside. He later summed those years for CNA in 2019: "Life was in an attap house and … the toilet was outside."

quote.text: Life was in an attap house and … the toilet was outside.

chapters.title: The bucket in the outhouse
chapters.turn: His mother was about to open his first school.
chapters.voice: An outside toilet shaped his earliest years.

chapters.body: Pancakes cooled on the neighbour's fruit pushcart for three nights. His mother, Tan Siam Kheng, had first tried selling pancakes through that pushcart, and when they did not sell she gave them away. With her last dollar she took a smocking-cushion class at the community centre, then taught six neighbours the same lesson for a dollar each. Jack, his brother and sister hand-copied her designs from blank exercise books bought at 10 cents into pattern books she sold for two dollars. When smocking went out of fashion she learned makeup at CK Tang, practised on Jack's sister and declared herself a wedding beautician. Over about 25 years she prepared more than 3,000 brides while his brother kept her accounts because she could not read or write. He later said: "I was glad to begin attending “Mother's Business School” at the age of six."

quote.text: I was glad to begin attending “Mother's Business School” at the age of six.

chapters.title: Mother's Business School
chapters.turn: School left him standing outside the door.
chapters.voice: His mother turned her last dollar into lessons for six neighbours.

chapters.body: He stood outside the classroom while the lesson went on inside. At school Jack was talkative and restless, and teachers repeatedly sent him to stand outside the classroom, so he missed lessons. His free textbooks did not arrive until April. He failed his O-levels, then two years later, in 1975, he graduated from vocational school with a hotel-management certificate. On his brother's advice he took work in construction as a site supervisor and was bad at it. The foreman asked his boss to take him off the site. He later told CNA in 2019: "The teacher always asked me to stand outside the classroom, so that was why I always failed."

quote.text: The teacher always asked me to stand outside the classroom, so that was why I always failed.

chapters.title: Outside the classroom door
chapters.turn: Selling suited him better than supervising.
chapters.voice: He missed the lessons happening behind the door.

chapters.body: The bank called about a bounced cheque. Jack had moved into selling building materials, became his department's top salesman, and an investor persuaded him to start his own company. In 1984 he founded Besco Building Supplies. He could not read accounts and only learned cash had run out when the bank called. Soon after he under-priced a Raffles City tender by S$1.1 million. After a week of worry he kept asking himself "just started business and immediately going bankrupt?" Then he confessed the error to the owners, who gave him the contract at the higher price if he used a German manufacturer. In what he calls blissful ignorance he formed a consortium to buy a S$30 million brick factory across the Causeway, then built 14 terrace houses at Rosyth Terrace and a 28-unit block on Meyer Road. He was a millionaire at 29.

quote.text: just started business and immediately going bankrupt?

chapters.title: The S$1.1 million mistake
chapters.turn: Then he rushed to save old voices.
chapters.voice: A costly error turned into his first break.

chapters.body: The reels sat at Hillview with demolition near. Jack learned that Rediffusion's dialect audio archive was still inside the building before it was demolished. A contact offered him everything for a price he later recalled as "You can have everything you want for $2,000." He paid the $2,000 for the archive. He was given only a day to collect it before the building came down. He moved quickly to take away what he could in the time allowed. Years later he donated over 4,700 reels to the National Archives. What had been stored in one building before demolition survived because he acted before the deadline.

quote.text: You can have everything you want for $2,000.

chapters.title: Reels at Hillview
chapters.turn: A crisis soon made him question his work.
chapters.voice: He had a day to save thousands of voices.

chapters.body: The fifteen properties were suddenly worth half. Jack had persuaded developers with a French supplier's clay tiles that a Mediterranean look would lift house prices, and within three years the firm dominated the market. Then the Asian financial crisis forced him to retrench staff and halved the value of his 15 properties, and he held on. He felt useless at work during those months. Around then he heard a speech arguing that a society's graciousness could be measured by the cleanliness of its toilets, and the idea stayed with him. Staff and peers called the toilet idea crazy. In December 1998 he founded the Restroom Association of Singapore. He told his wife that after the recession he would quit business for social work because it felt more fulfilling, explaining at the office: "When I come to the office, I don't feel useful. I feel like a failure."

quote.text: When I come to the office, I don't feel useful. I feel like a failure.

chapters.title: Fifteen houses at half price
chapters.turn: He decided to take toilets worldwide.
chapters.voice: Failure at the office pointed him toward toilets.

chapters.body: Laughter greeted the word toilet. On 19 November 2001 Jack founded the World Toilet Organization, and its founding date became World Toilet Day. Talking about toilets was taboo and people laughed at him, so he made toilet humour his brand and became known as Mr Toilet. He told audiences in figures he often repeated: "We go to the toilet six to eight times a day and spend three full years of our lives inside the toilet" In 2004 he stepped down as chief executive of Besco, his first company, to give the cause most of his time. The jokes opened rooms that polite language had not opened, and he kept using them.

quote.text: We go to the toilet six to eight times a day and spend three full years of our lives inside the toilet

chapters.title: Mr Toilet
chapters.voice: He laughed first so others would listen.

chapters.body: The award arrived in 2008. TIME named Jack one of its Heroes of the Environment. In 2011 he founded the BoP Hub to design businesses for the world's poorest. Donors still avoided the brown issue, and one of Asia's biggest banks told him funding him would hurt its image. He kept working without pay, and by 2022 he had worked unpaid for 21 years because donors avoided the issue. The recognition widened the rooms he could enter but did not pay a salary. He pushed faster anyway, living by the rule he gave in 2022: "Life is short. Every day is one less, so we need to be working faster"

quote.text: Life is short. Every day is one less, so we need to be working faster

chapters.title: The bank that said no
chapters.turn: Then the world gave toilets a day.
chapters.voice: A bank praised his work and turned him down.

chapters.body: The resolution passed on 24 July 2013. That day the UN General Assembly adopted Singapore's Sanitation for All resolution, making 19 November UN World Toilet Day. Tatler counted 122 countries that co-sponsored it. That same year the World Toilet Organization was granted consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council. He welcomed the decision in plain words he used that July: "There is nothing wrong with going to the toilet." The date gave the cause a place on the calendar, and the status gave his group a standing that let it keep returning to the same rooms.

quote.text: There is nothing wrong with going to the toilet.

chapters.title: A day at the UN
chapters.turn: Cameras soon followed him across continents.
chapters.voice: A local date became a world date.

chapters.body: The scooter rolled into frame. Filmmaker Lily Zepeda followed Jack for five years across Singapore, India, China and the United States for Mr. Toilet: The World's #2 Man. On screen he rode a scooter, combed his hair with a toilet brush and swam with a poo-emoji float. The film also showed tension with some WTO board members. At home his collection of toilets appeared in CNA's Money Mind profile. The documentary premiered at Hot Docs, North America's largest documentary festival, in April 2019 and opened in New York on 22 November 2019. The humour stayed on camera, but the strain behind the work stayed there too.
chapters.title: Mr. Toilet on film
chapters.turn: An old report card got a new reading.
chapters.voice: He combed his hair with a toilet brush on camera.

chapters.body: The suggestion came from his daughter. At about 65 Jack's daughter, a psychology student at SMU, told him she thought he had ADHD. He began to read his schoolboy restlessness differently after years of talk and restless energy at school. That same year the University of Strathclyde awarded him an honorary doctorate. He framed the lesson he would give his younger self in words he later repeated: "his quirks were actually his strengths" At home he lived with his wife, whom he married in 1990 after a first marriage in 1989 ended in divorce after a year, and their four children, two sons and two daughters. The restless boy and the honorary doctor were the same person.

quote.text: his quirks were actually his strengths

chapters.title: The boy outside the door, again
chapters.turn: He still kept dozens of jobs going at once.

chapters.body: The centre rose in Kampong Ubi. Jack built a S$10 million, 65,000 sq ft centre there, renamed the SDG Centre and financed mostly by a bank loan. Inside it held a kitchen to train single mothers. At 68 he said he ran 80 to 100 projects at once and lived with his wife and four children. The building gave his many projects one address. The kitchen gave single mothers a place to learn. The household gave the pace of those years a private shape, with work and home staying close together through long days.
chapters.title: Eighty projects at once
chapters.turn: The kitchen light stayed on after hours.

conflicts.choice: Follows Sim's own account of his mother as a wedding beautician who built a business; does not call her a housewife.
Uses 1984 per CNA; does not use 1982.
Uses adoption on 24 July 2013 with 122 co-sponsors; does not use 2012 with 120.
Uses second of three children; drops unverified youngest claim.
Omits disputed 15 versus 16 count of companies entirely.
Omits names and titles of politicians; refers only to a speech about clean toilets.
